title: Candy Corn Bag

drivers.name: Price increase (2.4%)
drivers.evidence: Price rose from $3.76 to $3.85. Past promotions show price elasticity; higher price reduces demand. No promotion in this week, so no uplift. Historical price hikes without promotions reduce sales. Applied conservative -10% adjustment.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 5.8. No events are scheduled. The price increased 2.4% to $3.85, above the regular $3.76. Past promotions show a median uplift of x2.15, but noise-adjusted is x1.52. The most recent promotion (Easter, 2026-03-30) was 25% off, featured, and produced x1.4 vs baseline—lower than historical average, suggesting diminishing returns. The price increase is a demand reducer. No past Mother's Day week before the event showed a meaningful effect (noise-adjusted x1.0). No driver justifies moving the median. The classical model’s x1.0 is correct. Spread remains baseline.

brief:
PRODUCT: Candy Corn Bag | category Candy | Store #12 (Austin, TX)
TARGET WEEK: 2026-04-27 to 2026-05-03 (next week)

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 3.85 (+2.4% vs regular price 3.76)

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 5.8 | 5%-95%: 0.0 - 14.9 | 10%-90%: 0.0 - 12.3

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-73% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
